title: What is known about 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its run is an odometer with three wheels; it can only halt at the moment the slowest wheel turns over, and only if the fastest one is at one exact position then.
verdict: The question is open. Every time the head reaches a new cell on the right in state B the tape is S(c, a, b) = (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0, and a three-line rule (checked against direct simulation) gives the next one. The machine halts only at a reset (c = 0 and 2b ≥ a) with b = a/2 exactly.

Why a halt is unlikely. The rule run for 108 macro steps from the start makes 38 resets, none halting; the left block now has tens of millions of cells. At a reset b is spread over about a/3 possible values, one of which halts, and resets grow roughly geometrically, so the chance of any future halt is of the order of 10−7.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,166 cells have been visited and 3,725 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The odometer rule
claims.text: For S(c, a, b) = 0^∞ (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0 0^∞ with a even and a ≥ 2, the next right-end visit in state B is: if 2b < a, S(c, a − 2b, 2b + 1) (the right block doubles, eating 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c ≥ 1, apply the rule to (c − 1, 2a + 4, max(b − a/2 − 1, 0)) (a carry: one 10 of the left block becomes 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c = 0, halt when b = a/2 and otherwise apply the rule to (a, 4, b − a/2 − 1) (a reset: the 1s become the new left block). Checked against direct simulation for all c < 6, even 2 ≤ a < 30, b < 34 (2,856 configurations), and on every such visit in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps of the run, which first reaches S(0, 4, 1) at step 43.

claims.title: 38 resets, no halt
claims.text: The rule iterated 10<sup>8</sup> times from S(0, 4, 1): 38 resets, at none of which b = a/2; the left blocks they create grow from 2, 8, 4, 24, 52, … to 44,140,926 at the 38th.

claims.title: A halt has probability about 10<sup>−7</sup>
claims.text: A reset follows a doubling step from (a′, b′) with 2b′ < a′ ≤ 6b′ + 2, so b′ takes about a′/3 values and exactly one gives b = a/2. With resets at pool sizes in the tens of millions and growing, the sum of the remaining chances is of the order of 10<sup>−7</sup>.

claims.title: Does a reset ever land on b = a/2?
claims.text: Open: nothing known controls the position of the fast wheel at the resets.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. The tape is an odometer with three wheels: a fast one that doubles, a middle one that ticks down, and a slow one that resets. The machine can only halt at a reset, and only if the fast wheel is on one exact value at that moment. In 38 resets that has never happened, and the target keeps getting smaller.

facts.text: The macro rule, checked against simulation.

sections.heading: Three wheels
html: Each time the head pushes the tape one cell further right in state B, the tape reads (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1: a left block of c pairs, a pool of a ones, and a right block of b pairs.
• Fast wheel. If the pool is big enough (2b < a), one sweep doubles the right block, b ↦ 2b + 1, paying 2b ones from the pool.
• Middle wheel. If the pool is too small and c ≥ 1, one 10 of the left block is turned into ones: the pool becomes 2a + 4 and b drops by a/2 + 1; then the fast wheel tries again.

• Slow wheel. If the pool is too small and the left block is empty, the whole pool becomes the new left block (c = a), a new pool of 4 starts, and b drops by a/2 + 1 — unless b is exactly a/2, and then the machine halts.

So the run is a sequence of resets, each one creating a left block as long as the pool was. From blank tape the first left blocks are 2, 8, 4, 24, 52, 44, 120, …; after 108 steps of the odometer there have been 38 resets and the latest left block is 44,140,926 pairs long.

At a reset the fast wheel can be on any of roughly a/3 positions, and only one halts. The chances shrink as the blocks grow, so the total chance that the machine ever halts is tiny (around one in ten million) — but nobody can rule it out.

explainer.title: An odometer that might stop on one exact number

summary: An odometer: (10)^b doubles while it eats a pool of 1s, a carry turns one 10 of the left block (10)^c into 1s, and when c is empty the pool becomes the new left block; it halts only if a reset hits b = a/2 exactly. No halt in 38 resets; heuristically about a 10^-7 chance of ever halting.
